decisions.decision: Correctness, rules-fidelity, and deterministic local state always outrank visual polish whenever they compete for build/complexity budget, and any such trade-off must be logged rather than silently resolved.
decisions.rationale: The original prompt itself states visual ambition must not cost playability/correctness; this fleet has a documented history of visual ambition winning while correctness quietly breaks.
rejected_alternatives: Letting a later phase silently ship the prettier but rules-broken version
constraints: Every later phase must justify any cut to gameplay/state logic; cuts come out of the art system first

decisions.decision: The 52-card face system (+ back) must be a systematic/generative/parametric design — shared type and icon components plus programmatic layout rules — not 52 independently hand-illustrated cards.
decisions.rationale: Hand-illustrating 52 unique faces to a consistent standard is a scope trap likely to yield a few great cards and many generic ones, which itself fails the prompt's own 'looks like a stock tutorial' test.
rejected_alternatives: 52 independently hand-illustrated card faces
constraints: Face system must be visually consistent across the full deck and card back in one shared visual grammar

decisions.decision: All persistence is strictly single-device local storage (UserDefaults/FileManager/SwiftData) with no CloudKit container; no iCloud or cross-device sync of saved game, stats, or settings.
decisions.rationale: Zero-network/zero-account constraint is interpreted to forbid any sync mechanism even though CloudKit-synced data would still technically be 'local' per device — closes a loophole someone could exploit later thinking it's harmless.
rejected_alternatives: Allowing CloudKit sync of save/stats/settings since the data itself originates locally
constraints: No CloudKit container, no NSUbiquitousKeyValueStore, no networking APIs anywhere in the codebase

decisions.decision: Stats and best-time are tracked separately for draw-1 vs draw-3, never combined.
decisions.rationale: Draw-1 and draw-3 have materially different win rates and completion times; a combined metric would misrepresent the player's actual performance.
rejected_alternatives: Single combined stats/best-time pool across both draw modes
constraints: Stats screen must present or select per-mode figures, not an averaged/merged number

decisions.decision: When the timer is off, best time displays as 'N/A', never a fabricated 0:00 or a stale prior value.
decisions.rationale: Fleet-wide rule against claiming outcomes/state that didn't truly happen; showing a fake time would be lying about data that was never captured.
rejected_alternatives: Showing 0:00 or the last recorded time when timer is disabled
constraints: Stats screen must branch explicitly on timer-enabled state per session

decisions.decision: Card back selection can change live at any time; changing draw mode (1 vs 3) requires starting a new game.
decisions.rationale: Card back is purely cosmetic and safe to swap mid-game; draw mode changes the legal deal/hand semantics, so applying it mid-game would corrupt in-progress state.
rejected_alternatives: Allowing draw-mode changes to apply instantly mid-game
constraints: Settings screen must gate draw-mode changes behind a new-game action or confirmation

decisions.decision: Klondike is locked as single-deck, 7 tableau columns, 4 foundations (one per suit), ascending same-suit foundation moves, alternating-color descending tableau sequences, and King-only placement into empty tableau columns.
decisions.rationale: Removes ambiguity in the prompt so later phases build against one unambiguous rule set instead of rediscovering rules mid-implementation.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving rule variants (e.g., multi-deck, unrestricted empty-column placement) open for later interpretation
constraints: All move-validation logic must conform to this exact rule set

decisions.decision: Stock cycling/reshuffle behavior is fixed by explicit settings semantics and documented in-app; no implicit unlimited reshuffle unless a setting explicitly enables it.
decisions.rationale: Prevents an ambiguous or silently-changed stock-recycle rule from being 'discovered' during implementation.
rejected_alternatives: Implicit unlimited stock reshuffling as a hidden default
constraints: Stock cycling behavior must be stated wherever rules/help content exists

decisions.decision: The game timer starts on the first action of a game and pauses when the app is backgrounded, unless the user has disabled timing in settings.
decisions.rationale: Locks otherwise-ambiguous timer semantics so stats/best-time behavior is deterministic and testable.
rejected_alternatives: Timer running continuously regardless of app state
Timer starting at deal instead of first action
constraints: Timer logic must respect app lifecycle (background/foreground) and the timer-on/off setting

decisions.decision: Non-goals are locked: no multiplayer/social/leaderboards, no other solitaire variants, no IAP/ads/monetization, no accounts/sign-in, no analytics/telemetry/crash SDKs, no Game Center/achievements, no iCloud sync, portrait-first only.
decisions.rationale: Prevents both scope creep (adding unrequested features) and silent scope-cutting (dropping required ones) by fixing the boundary explicitly.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving non-goals implicit and inferred per phase
constraints: Any later phase proposing one of these features must be flagged as violating the contract

decisions.decision: Production-ready means: full start-to-finish playability with correct legal-move enforcement in both draw modes, multi-step undo with exact state restoration, fresh real-RNG shuffle every new game, win fires only on a true win, stats/settings persist across relaunch, both appearances fully themed with no literal colors/fonts outside the theme file, and zero placeholder screens among Game/Stats/Settings.
decisions.rationale: Compiles-and-runs is not an acceptable bar for this app given the fleet's documented history of blank-screen and hardcoded-color failures; this app gets a stricter, named bar.
rejected_alternatives: Treating successful build/run as sufficient evidence of done
constraints: Blank-screen and hardcoded-literal-color/font findings are automatic rejects for this app

decisions.decision: Haptics requirements are verified by checking the code for correct haptic API calls at the correct trigger points (move accepted, move rejected if implemented, win), not by an automated build/screenshot check.
decisions.rationale: Haptic output cannot be observed from a static build artifact or screenshot, so verification method must be named explicitly to avoid the requirement being silently waved through or silently failed.
rejected_alternatives: Treating haptics as unverifiable and dropping it from acceptance checks
constraints: Verification phase must inspect source for haptic trigger call sites, not just simulator behavior

decisions.decision: Target audience is framed as two overlapping segments: casual quick-session players who want zero-friction reliability, and a design-literate audience that will screenshot-compare the app against premium/award-caliber visual bars.
decisions.rationale: The prompt itself asks for both real playability and award-level visual distinctiveness, implying both audiences must be satisfied simultaneously rather than trading one off for the other.
rejected_alternatives: Treating this as a single generic casual-puzzle audience
constraints: Design and UX decisions must satisfy reliability-first expectations even while pursuing visual ambition

decisions.decision: Information architecture is a TabView with Game, Stats, and Settings as shallow peer destinations, with resume-active-game as the primary path into the app.
decisions.rationale: Usage is genuinely three peer surfaces with shallow depth; a tab-first shell keeps a low-cognitive-load path back into the in-progress game, matching HIG guidance for peer sections.
rejected_alternatives: Custom chrome or a single-screen-with-overlays structure
constraints: Game must load directly into the resumed/active game state, not an intermediate menu

decisions.decision: Legibility of the bespoke rank/suit glyph system at true on-device card size (7 tableau columns in portrait, ~45-50pt card width) is a hard gate that must be validated before the card art system is considered settled.
decisions.rationale: An illegible rank/suit glyph at actual gameplay size is a correctness/gameplay bug (player can't identify the card), not merely an aesthetic shortfall, and directly risks failing the brief's own 'looks like a stock tutorial' test in the opposite direction (illegible custom art).
rejected_alternatives: Judging the card art system only at mockup/zoomed scale
constraints: Design phase must explicitly test/confirm glyph legibility at native card size before the face system is locked

decisions.decision: Touch targets for card dragging must include hit-testing padding beyond the visual card bounds, and multi-card run dragging plus z-order stability are named as the top technical interaction risk for the first build.
decisions.rationale: Narrow tableau columns plus precise drop-target detection is exactly the kind of interaction that looks fine in a demo but fails under a real thumb; repeated mis-tap snap-backs read as janky, undermining the prompt's core 'tactile' goal.
rejected_alternatives: Relying on exact visual card bounds for touch/drop targets
constraints: Interaction/build phases must budget extra hit-area beyond rendered card edges

decisions.decision: Custom card rendering must explicitly re-implement accessibility that system controls give for free: honor accessibilityReduceMotion for spring/flip/drag animation, avoid color-only suit differentiation, and provide explicit VoiceOver labels (e.g. 'Seven of Hearts, tableau column 3, face up') for every card.
decisions.rationale: A fully custom, non-SF-Symbols card renderer does not inherit accessibility behavior the way system components do; it must be deliberately wired in.
rejected_alternatives: Treating accessibility as automatically covered because the app uses SwiftUI
constraints: Build phase must implement VoiceOver labels and reduce-motion fallbacks for all card views and animations

decisions.decision: Stock cycling defaults to unlimited redeal (waste recycles back into stock and can be redrawn indefinitely); a capped number of passes is out of scope unless a later phase explicitly argues for it.
decisions.rationale: The prompt_contract phase required stock-cycling behavior to be explicit but left the actual value undecided; unlimited recycling is the more common casual-app default and the simplest to implement correctly, closing a gap before implementation-time improvisation fills it inconsistently.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving stock cycling behavior undecided until the build phase
Defaulting to a limited-pass variant
constraints: Game rules/help content and stock-pile interaction logic must implement and document unlimited redeal unless explicitly superseded

decisions.decision: Persisted game state must represent logical state (which pile each card belongs to, face-up/face-down) independent of in-flight animation position, so an app kill mid-drag or mid-flip does not produce a relaunch state that looks corrupted.
decisions.rationale: iOS can terminate the app at any point, including mid-animation; if persistence is tied to visual/animation state rather than logical state, relaunch can show a mismatch that reads as a data-integrity bug even though the underlying logic was never actually broken.
rejected_alternatives: Persisting state snapshots that can be captured mid-animation
constraints: Save/load logic must only ever serialize settled logical game state, never an in-progress animation frame

decisions.decision: The first build's signature visual/interaction hook is the deal/flip animation, not multi-card run-drag physics.
decisions.rationale: The deal/flip is the first thing every user sees and can be made to feel premium without first solving the harder and riskier multi-card drag/z-order problem, letting the team ship a real signature moment early while treating run-dragging as a follow-on hardening task.
rejected_alternatives: Making multi-card drag physics the primary signature interaction from the start
constraints: Design/build phases should invest first-build polish budget in deal/flip motion before perfecting run-drag physics

decisions.decision: The first build explicitly avoids scope creep into Game Center, widgets, or Live Activities even though they are native-feeling iOS affordances.
decisions.rationale: These features either directly violate the no-network/no-accounts contract constraint (Game Center) or are simply not requested and would divert build budget from the correctness-first core.
rejected_alternatives: Adding these as 'free' native polish since they feel idiomatic to iOS
constraints: Any later phase proposing these features must be flagged as out of scope per DEC-prompt_contract-010

decisions.decision: This prompt is a single-app build, not a portfolio parent: one project (solitaire-atelier) with Game, Stats, and Settings as in-app tabs, no sibling child projects, no portfolio-json manifest emitted.
decisions.rationale: The prompt requests exactly one product — a native iOS Klondike solitaire game — with no second category, variant, or companion app implied; treating sub-surfaces as separate apps would be inventing scope the prompt never asked for.
rejected_alternatives: Splitting Stats into a separate app
Splitting Settings into a separate app
Shipping a card-back/theme pack as a separate companion app
constraints: No portfolio-json manifest required for this run
All functionality must live in one sibling project: solitaire-atelier
Any later phase proposing a sibling/companion project must be flagged as violating this decision

decisions.decision: Selected app locked as: category Games/Card, slug solitaire-atelier, promise 'a fully playable, rules-correct Klondike solitaire with local-only persistence, tap/drag interaction, undo, win detection, and premium custom card visuals with local stats/settings', target user casual-to-premium mobile solitaire players who need reliability and high visual fidelity, build=true.
decisions.rationale: Restates the single product as a concrete, buildable spec so later phases build against one named app rather than re-deriving scope.
rejected_alternatives: Renaming the slug away from the existing working-directory name
constraints: build flag is true — production-ready bar applies, not a sketch/prototype

decisions.decision: Product promise is locked as: a single native iOS Klondike solitaire game with fully correct rules, a bespoke tactile card system, 100% on-device operation, and no claimed outcome that didn't truly happen.
decisions.rationale: Compresses every earlier-phase constraint into one testable sentence a developer can build against.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving the promise as a longer multi-clause description without a single anchor sentence
constraints: Any later phase's feature proposal must trace back to this one-sentence promise or be flagged as scope drift

decisions.decision: Primary user is framed as two overlapping scenarios sharing one requirement: a casual player wanting a fast, interruption-tolerant five-to-fifteen-minute session, and a design-literate player judging first-screen quality — both require zero-friction resume into the active game with no interstitial start/menu screen.
decisions.rationale: Both audiences named in product_research converge on the same IA requirement (resume-first, no menu screen), so this phase locks that as a concrete build requirement rather than leaving it as separate audience framing.
rejected_alternatives: A traditional start/menu screen shown before entering the active game
constraints: App must launch directly into the resumed game state or a fresh deal, never an intermediate menu

decisions.decision: The core loop explicitly includes two named terminal states beyond just 'win': a true win (all foundations complete) and a stuck board (no legal moves remain), both of which must be explicitly surfaced to the player rather than left ambiguous.
decisions.rationale: Klondike frequently ends in a stalemate, not a win; the original prompt never mentions this state, but silently omitting it would leave players unable to tell whether they're stuck or the app is broken.
rejected_alternatives: Only designing for the win state and treating stuck-board detection as out of scope
constraints: Build phase must implement no-legal-moves detection and a corresponding UI state, in addition to the win state

decisions.decision: Undo is designed as an inline safety net within the single game session (multi-step, restores exact prior state), not a separate history-browsing mode or screen.
decisions.rationale: Matches how a player actually uses undo mid-hand ('take that back') rather than treating it as a distinct feature surface.
rejected_alternatives: A separate undo/history screen or log
constraints: Undo UI must be reachable from within the active game view, not a navigation destination

decisions.decision: When a visual/art-direction idea conflicts with a rules-correctness or state-integrity requirement, the rules/state requirement wins and the trade-off must be logged rather than silently resolved in the art's favor.
decisions.rationale: Restates and operationalizes DEC-prompt_contract-001 as a concrete decision rule for this phase's scope document, since the original prompt itself warns visual ambition must not cost playability.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving this as an abstract principle without restating it as an enforceable phase decision
constraints: Any phase or build step that trades correctness for visual polish must document the trade-off explicitly

decisions.decision: Because there is no interstitial start screen, the cold-launch deal/flip animation and card rendering are treated as the least forgiving, highest-stakes moment in the app, not just the nicest one — the mandatory unskippable first three seconds of every launch.
decisions.rationale: The resume-first, no-menu-screen decision (DEC-initial_discussion-002) means there is no loading screen to hide rough edges in the signature animation; any hitch is visible on every cold launch.
rejected_alternatives: Treating the deal/flip animation as a nice-to-have polish item with normal priority
constraints: Build/QA must specifically regression-test the cold-launch deal animation, not just mid-session interactions

decisions.decision: Success criteria for this app are locked as: deterministic legal/illegal move validation in both draw modes; full playable start-to-win path; explicit stuck-board detection; multi-step exact-state undo; crash/relaunch-safe persistence of logical (not animation) state; per-draw-mode stats with 'N/A' best time when timing is off; and rank/suit legibility at true on-device card size as a pass/fail gate.
decisions.rationale: Turns the product promise into criteria a build can actually be checked against instead of subjective 'looks good' judgments.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving success criteria as qualitative/aesthetic judgments only
constraints: Verification phases must check each of these criteria explicitly before declaring the app done

decisions.decision: Confirmed and closed: solitaire-atelier ships with zero monetization surface in v1 (no IAP, no subscription tier, no ads); 'paid value' is reframed as the retention/trust value of a free, ad-free, tracking-free download rather than a functional subscription unlock.
decisions.rationale: DEC-prompt_contract-010 already locked 'no monetization' as a non-goal three phases ago; inventing a subscription now to satisfy the generic phase template would silently violate an existing decision rather than build on it.
rejected_alternatives: Inventing a speculative 'Atelier Pro' subscription SKU (cloud backup, solver-assisted review) as part of this brief
Treating the phase template's 'subscription value' requirement as mandatory and overriding the locked non-goal
constraints: Any future subscription/IAP proposal must explicitly reopen and supersede DEC-prompt_contract-010, not be treated as pre-approved by this brief

decisions.decision: Target user is locked as two overlapping groups with a shared zero-forgiveness trait: casual players burned by freemium solitaire ads/paywalls/streak-guilt mechanics, and design-literate players who judge and screenshot the app on first-screen quality alone.
decisions.rationale: Both groups converge on the same design constraint even though their motivations differ: any jank (a wrong-feeling drag, a rules bug) is immediately and permanently punished by both, so there is no slack in the execution bar.
rejected_alternatives: Treating this as a single generic casual-puzzle audience without the zero-forgiveness framing
constraints: Design/build phases must treat interaction jank and rules bugs as maximum-severity, not minor polish issues

decisions.decision: Competitive wedge is explicitly framed as non-defensible via moat/data/network-effects — its only real protection is sustained execution quality (rules correctness, real undo, a card system that stays legible and tactile at native size) since a competitor could clone the art direction.
decisions.rationale: Naming the wedge honestly prevents the brief from overclaiming a durable competitive advantage that doesn't actually exist given the locked no-accounts/no-network/no-social constraints.
rejected_alternatives: Describing the wedge as inherently durable/defensible
constraints: Later phases should not treat v1 shipping as sufficient; ongoing execution quality is the actual competitive claim

decisions.decision: Local-only persistence's failure mode on reinstall/device migration (silent loss of stats, streak, and in-progress game) is accepted as correct behavior given the locked constraints, but must be disclosed via one line of Settings copy so the app isn't silently vague about data durability.
decisions.rationale: Local-only storage was already locked (DEC-prompt_contract-003), but the user-facing consequence of that constraint had never been named or given a disclosure requirement.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving this trade-off unstated and undiscovered until a user complaint surfaces it
constraints: Settings screen must include a short line disclosing that stats/progress are device-local only

decisions.decision: Reaffirmed as the phase's sharpened framing: if any later phase must cut scope under time pressure, the cut must always come from visual polish, never from move-validation, undo fidelity, or win/stuck-board detection.
decisions.rationale: Restates DEC-prompt_contract-001/DEC-initial_discussion-005 with a concrete example of the actual failure mode (a false illegal-move rejection or false stuck-board detection makes the app worse than the ad-laden competitors it's trying to beat) so it isn't just an abstract principle by this point in the pipeline.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving this as a restated abstract principle without a concrete failure example
constraints: Any phase making a correctness-vs-polish trade-off must log it explicitly, per DEC-initial_discussion-005

decisions.decision: v1's growth/sharing feature is a one-tap native share sheet on the win screen that shares a rendered image of the completed board (with a solve-time caption), and explicitly excludes any challenge-seed/replay mechanic.
decisions.rationale: A shareable seed requires the shuffle to be reproducible from that seed across devices and OS versions, but Swift's SystemRandomNumberGenerator is not a documented, versioned algorithm and offers no such guarantee — supporting seeded replay would require a second, hand-rolled deterministic RNG living alongside the real-shuffle path, creating dual shuffle code paths that risk violating the locked 'fresh real-RNG shuffle every new game' correctness guarantee (DEC-prompt_contract-011) and spending correctness-tier build budget on an unproven behavioral bet (no evidence players want to compare identical deals).
rejected_alternatives: Challenge-seed/replay share feature requiring a second deterministic RNG and seeded-deal code path
Zero built-in sharing feature at all, relying purely on unprompted organic screenshots
constraints: Build phase implements only image-rendering + UIActivityViewController on the win screen — no new RNG, no seed encoding/decoding, no deal-replay logic
Any future seeded-challenge/replay feature must be proposed and scoped as its own decision, not treated as pre-approved by this brief

decisions.decision: The first build slice is frozen to draw-1 only; draw-3 is explicitly sequenced as the second increment after draw-1's move-legality and persistence correctness are proven, not cut permanently.
decisions.rationale: Both agents independently converged on this to reduce state-space complexity so correctness invariants (legal-move validation, undo, persistence) can be verified on the simpler mode before adding draw-mode-switching complexity.
rejected_alternatives: Building both draw-1 and draw-3 in the first slice
constraints: Build phase implements draw-1 gameplay only in this slice; draw-mode setting/switcher is out of scope until a later increment

decisions.decision: Multi-card run-drag (dragging a stacked sequence in one gesture) is deferred out of this slice; whatever interaction model is chosen (tap-only or tap+single-card-drag, still unresolved) only ever moves one card or an auto-routed single legal move at a time.
decisions.rationale: Both agents agree multi-card run-drag is the hardest unsolved interaction risk per product_research and should not be attempted before single-card correctness is proven.
rejected_alternatives: Building multi-card run-drag in the first slice
constraints: Build phase must not attempt stacked-run dragging in this slice

decisions.decision: The win-screen share-image feature and any subscription/ads/economy surface are excluded from this slice entirely.
decisions.rationale: Both agents agree these are new/optional scope relative to the core rules-engine proof this slice exists to deliver, and per DEC-per_app_product_brief-006 the share feature was already scoped as a later, separate, low-risk addition, not a day-one requirement.
rejected_alternatives: Including the win-screen share sheet in slice 1
constraints: Build phase does not implement image rendering or UIActivityViewController integration in this slice

decisions.decision: This slice must implement full multi-step undo, both terminal states (true win and stuck board) with explicit detection, and persistence of logical (not animation) game state across backgrounding and relaunch — none of these are reduced or stubbed.
decisions.rationale: Both agents agree these are the correctness-critical elements the whole slice exists to de-risk, consistent with the locked ordering rule that correctness always outranks polish.
rejected_alternatives: Deferring stuck-board detection or multi-step undo to a later increment
constraints: Verification of this phase's output must explicitly check undo-across-a-sequence, stuck-board detection accuracy, and relaunch-safe logical state restore

decisions.decision: Settings and Stats screens (UI) are excluded from slice 1 entirely; only the game screen ships in this increment.
decisions.rationale: Both agents converged that shipping these tabs now either means forbidden stub placeholders or pulls in edge-case complexity (timer toggle persistence, card-back state) before the core rules engine is proven, which doesn't serve this slice's purpose of de-risking correctness and the signature hook.
rejected_alternatives: Shipping Settings/Stats tabs with real but narrowed data in slice 1 (Claude's round-1 position, since withdrawn)
constraints: Build phase implements no TabView shell and no Settings/Stats screens in this slice

decisions.decision: The cold-launch deal/flip animation must be a real, non-placeholder implementation in slice 1 — spring-based per-card deal sequencing and a genuine flip reveal using the actual bespoke card art and real timing — not a basic or throwaway transition; later increments can still refine micro-polish (parallax, ambient shadow tuning) on top of it.
decisions.rationale: Both agents converged on this after Codex revised its round-1 'basic transition' position: because there is no menu screen to hide behind (DEC-initial_discussion-006), this slice is the only chance to find out whether the signature hook actually works before more is built on top of unvalidated animation assumptions, and a placeholder would tell the team nothing.
rejected_alternatives: Shipping a basic/placeholder deal transition in slice 1 and deferring the real animation to a later increment
constraints: Build phase must implement the true deal/flip mechanics (per-card spring sequencing, real card art in the flip) even if final micro-polish is deferred

decisions.decision: Slice 1 silently records local game-event data (session start/end, elapsed seconds, undo count) from day one even though no Stats UI exists yet in this slice.
decisions.rationale: Both agents confirmed this in round 3: it's a data-loss-prevention measure that costs almost nothing (a struct appended to local storage on game start/end) and avoids a scenario where early dogfooding/playtesting sessions are permanently unrecoverable once the Stats screen is built in a later increment.
rejected_alternatives: Recording no game-event data until the Stats UI itself is built
constraints: Build phase adds a write-only local event-recording model tied to game start/end, with no UI surface and no dependency on Settings (defaults to timer-enabled, draw-1) in this slice

decisions.decision: Starting a New Game while an unfinished (not won, not stuck) game is in progress requires an explicit user confirmation before resetting state; it is never silent or implicit.
decisions.rationale: Both agents independently landed on this in round 1: destroying an active game without confirmation is a data-loss pattern, not a convenience, and conflicts with the app's own 'we tell you the truth about your data' positioning.
rejected_alternatives: Implicitly resetting to a fresh deal the moment New Game is tapped, with no confirmation step
constraints: Build phase must gate New Game behind a confirmation dialog whenever the current game is neither won nor already detected as stuck

decisions.decision: Tap-to-move is locked as: tapping a movable source card executes the move immediately if exactly one legal destination exists; if multiple legal destinations exist, all are highlighted and a confirming tap on one completes the move; if zero legal destinations exist, the app shows the same rejection feedback as a blocked move with nothing highlighted — all three cases routed through one shared move-validation/mutation function.
decisions.rationale: Silent auto-routing to a single destination would remove real strategic choice from Klondike (e.g. a card with two legal same-rank/color homes) and give an inconsistent accessibility story; requiring a second tap on every move would make the common single-destination case feel sluggish. This synthesis gets both instant feel for the common case and preserved player agency for the ambiguous case.
rejected_alternatives: Deterministic silent auto-routing to one destination via a fixed foundation/tableau priority rule
Requiring a confirming second tap on every move, including the single-legal-destination case
constraints: Build phase implements one shared canMove/attemptMove path for all three cases (single/multiple/zero legal destinations)
VoiceOver must expose the highlighted legal destinations as explicit accessibility actions when a tap resolves to more than one

decisions.decision: The deal/flip animation plays only on a genuinely fresh deal — first launch with no saved game, or an explicit New Game action — and never replays when a cold launch resumes an in-progress board.
decisions.rationale: The signature animation must not become a forced tax on every reopen, which would violate the zero-friction resume requirement (DEC-initial_discussion-002); the animation is a one-time presentation over already-computed logical state, not a replayable ritual.
rejected_alternatives: Replaying the deal/flip sequence on every cold launch regardless of whether the game is fresh or resumed
constraints: Deal animation logic must check for an existing in-progress saved game before deciding whether to play the sequence

decisions.decision: Draw-1 stuck-board detection is computed as a single static legality pass over every currently exposed tableau/foundation card plus every card in stock+waste treated as a potential waste top, with no simulation of stock-recycle order; this shortcut applies to draw-1 only and must not be reused unmodified for a future draw-3 increment.
decisions.rationale: Under unlimited redeal, a card's legality depends only on its own identity and the current board state, not on when it happens to surface as the waste top, so simulating cycling is unnecessary work that risks either an expensive-and-wrong or cheap-and-wrong (false-stuck) implementation.
rejected_alternatives: Simulating stock-recycle passes to determine reachability before declaring a stuck board
Checking only the current waste top, which would produce false stuck positives for cards still buried in stock
constraints: A future draw-3 increment must design its own stuck-detection approach rather than inheriting this static-pass shortcut

decisions.decision: The system LaunchScreen is themed to match the app's card-table background rather than left as the default white system launch screen.
decisions.rationale: Given this fleet's documented history of blank/placeholder-screen visual QA failures, and that the deal animation immediately following launch is the app's highest-stakes moment, a default white flash directly ahead of it would itself read as exactly the anti-pattern the app must avoid.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving the default system LaunchScreen unstyled
constraints: LaunchScreen storyboard/asset must use the app's theme background color, not system default

decisions.decision: The game timer starts on the first state-mutating player action — a confirmed move or a stock draw — not on the deal/flip animation and not on merely opening the app.
decisions.rationale: Locks DEC-prompt_contract-009's 'starts on first action' language to a literal, testable definition so a player who opens the app, watches the deal, and gets interrupted before touching anything isn't silently accruing elapsed time.
rejected_alternatives: Starting the timer on app open or on the deal animation itself
Starting the timer on a bare card selection that doesn't yet mutate state (proposed but not reconciled this round)
constraints: Timer-start logic must key off a completed move or stock draw event, not selection or animation events

decisions.decision: Persisted game state is written atomically (write to a temporary location, then swap) to prevent corruption from a mid-write app kill.
decisions.rationale: Both agents agreed this is real crash-safety engineering with no meaningful cost, distinct from and unlike the rejected encryption-layer question.
rejected_alternatives: Direct in-place writes to the persisted state file without a temp-then-swap step
constraints: Build phase must implement save operations as write-temp-then-atomic-replace, not direct overwrite

decisions.decision: Tap-to-move includes relocating a validly-stacked tableau run (the maximal face-up alternating-descending sequence starting at the tapped card) as a single unit through the same select-then-confirm mechanic already locked for single cards; 'multi-card run-drag deferred' (DEC-next_steps_small-002) is clarified to mean only the live interactive drag gesture is deferred, not this rules capability.
decisions.rationale: Canonical Klondike (DEC-prompt_contract-007) routinely requires moving a stacked run as one unit; restricting the move model to single cards only would make some legal, winnable boards undetectably unwinnable and would get falsely flagged as stuck by the stuck-detection algorithm locked in DEC-detailed_discussion-004. The run structure is always well-defined at selection time because every face-up stacked card only got there via an already-validated move, so this adds no new ambiguity or live-gesture machinery (no continuous touch tracking, no dynamic drop-target recomputation, no z-order conflicts).
rejected_alternatives: Restricting tap-to-move to single cards only in this slice, accepting that some legal run-relocation moves would be inexecutable and could cause false stuck-board detections
constraints: Build phase must compute the headmost card of a tapped run, validate/highlight its legal destinations exactly like a single card, and animate the whole run moving together on confirm, through the same shared attemptMove core
This does not reopen or reintroduce any live interactive drag gesture in this slice

decisions.decision: Local persistence uses no encryption layer of any kind — plain FileManager/UserDefaults/SwiftData only, with the atomic write-temp-then-swap behavior already locked in DEC-detailed_discussion-007 as the sole persistence-safety mechanism.
decisions.rationale: There is no PII, credential, or otherwise sensitive data in this app's persisted state; adding an encrypted-storage path (e.g. Keychain) would introduce new failure surface (locked-device access timing, key migration) to defend against a threat that doesn't exist for this data, spending engineering effort against the standing rule that correctness/reliability budget shouldn't go to unnecessary surface area.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving encryption as an optional 'use it if platform defaults offer it' soft clause
constraints: Build phase must not introduce a Keychain or other encrypted-storage dependency for game/settings/stats persistence

decisions.decision: The app is locked to portrait-only orientation at the project level for whatever device classes it ends up supporting, without adding an artificial iPhone-only device restriction; any broader device-class scoping (e.g. explicit iPad support) is left to the project's existing/default configuration and would require its own future decision, not one forced by this phase.
decisions.rationale: The real risk both agents cared about was avoiding a half-supported landscape layout, which a portrait-only lock addresses directly; inventing an iPhone-only device-class restriction as a side effect of that lock would be deciding a question (device support) that nobody actually raised or justified.
rejected_alternatives: Explicitly restricting the app to iPhone-only at the Xcode target/Info.plist level
constraints: Build phase locks supported orientations to portrait only, without altering supported device-class targeting beyond project defaults

decisions.decision: Settings and Stats ship as fully real, non-placeholder screens in this build (in a TabView shell with resume-first launch), not deferred to a hypothetical later increment.
decisions.rationale: No phase in this pipeline names a scheduled second build; treating 'slice 1' framing from next_steps_small/detailed_discussion as implying a guaranteed follow-on build would silently cut two screens the original prompt names explicitly and violate DEC-prompt_contract-011's zero-placeholder-screens bar.
rejected_alternatives: Deferring Settings/Stats UI to a 'could-have' increment with no scheduled phase to build it
constraints: Build phase must implement Game, Stats, and Settings as real TabView peers with resume-first launch into the active game
Stats/Settings must use the already-planned silent event-recording data model, not new placeholder data

decisions.decision: Draw-3 is a core, fully-working mode in this build, with its own stuck-detection approach: the same permissive static pass used for draw-1 (treat every stock/waste card as a hypothetical reachable card), explicitly documented as a conservative approximation rather than an exact proof, biased to avoid ever falsely declaring a board stuck when a legal move still exists.
decisions.rationale: Draw-3's card grouping makes exact reachability a real combinatorial problem this build's time budget shouldn't try to solve precisely; a false 'not stuck yet' just costs the player an extra draw, while a false 'you're stuck, game over' is a serious trust violation on an app whose core promise is not lying about the player's own data.
rejected_alternatives: Reusing the draw-1 static pass unmodified without acknowledging its exactness doesn't transfer
Attempting an exact stock-cycle-reachability simulation for draw-3 within this build
Shipping draw-3 as a UI toggle without a real, owned stuck-detection implementation
constraints: Build phase must implement and document draw-3 stuck-detection as a conservative approximation, distinct from draw-1's exact static pass
Verification must specifically test that draw-3 never falsely reports stuck when a legal move exists

decisions.decision: To afford building the full Game/Stats/Settings/draw-3 triad within this build's scope, the should/could tier is cut instead: win-screen share sheet, live interactive drag (single or multi-card), and extra card-back variants beyond the minimum are excluded from this build.
decisions.rationale: The hard, novel engineering risk in this app was always the rules engine, run-relocation logic, persistence integrity, and card-art legibility — Settings/Stats are comparatively cheap once the underlying event-recording data model exists (already planned from day one), so the scope trade should come from features not named by the original prompt, not from ones that are.
rejected_alternatives: Cutting Settings/Stats/draw-3 to afford should/could-tier polish items
Building both the full triad and the should/could tier without any scope reduction
constraints: Build phase excludes win-screen sharing, live drag gestures, and extra card-back variants from this build's scope

decisions.decision: Stats screen must show a real, honest empty state per draw mode before any game completes in that mode (e.g. '0 games played'), never a placeholder number, never the other mode's data, and never a blank view.
decisions.rationale: Directly applies the global empty/loading/success/error states rule and the no-fabricated-data rule to the specific case of a brand-new install or a mode that hasn't been played yet.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving the pre-first-game Stats state undefined or blank
constraints: Verification must check Stats screen behavior on first launch before any game is completed in each draw mode

decisions.decision: Changing the draw-mode setting while a game is in progress requires the same explicit confirmation pattern already locked for New Game: confirming discards the current game and starts a fresh deal in the new mode; canceling leaves both the setting and the in-progress game unchanged.
decisions.rationale: Draw mode change is functionally equivalent to starting a new game (DEC-prompt_contract-006 already requires draw-mode changes to be gated behind a new-game action), so it should reuse the identical confirmation UX rather than inventing a second pattern.
rejected_alternatives: Applying a draw-mode change silently and immediately, corrupting or force-resetting the in-progress game with no confirmation
constraints: Build phase must route draw-mode setting changes through the same confirmation dialog component as New Game

decisions.decision: The app's design language is locked as 'Baize & Vellum': a deep green felt table as the dominant surface, matte parchment-toned card stock with embossed bespoke rank/suit glyphs, and aged pewter reduced to small hardware accents rather than a dominant metal surface.
decisions.rationale: A brass/foil-forward palette (the earlier 'Brass & Baize' pitch, even with a pip-zone guardrail) risks reading as casino/loot-box shiny, which directly undercuts this app's locked competitive positioning as the honest, non-monetized alternative to freemium solitaire apps; embossed matte vellum gives cards real depth without a specular highlight that could wash out the rank/suit glyph at the ~45-50pt legibility gate.
rejected_alternatives: Velvet Tabletop Atelier (vellum gradients, matte stock, embossed glyphs, restrained contrast bands, no felt-table identity)
Brass & Baize (brass/foil as a dominant or restrained-but-present surface treatment)
constraints: The rank/suit glyph zone must remain flat, high-contrast, and free of texture/gradient/specular treatments
Metal accents are limited to small hardware details (foundation-pile ring, card-back border piping), never a dominant surface

decisions.decision: Light and dark mode are art-directed as two distinct lighting scenes on the same table, not a palette inversion: light mode is the table by daylight through a window (cooler, brighter felt, properly grey pewter, soft diffuse shadow); dark mode is the same table lit only by a desk lamp at night (warmer, more saturated green pooling toward near-black at the edges, a single directional light source, warm dim pewter).
decisions.rationale: A vague 'restrained contrast bands' description isn't specific enough for a SwiftUI developer to build a Theme.swift from; naming two concrete lighting scenarios gives both appearances a genuinely different lighting logic rather than an inverted color set.
rejected_alternatives: Generic 'restrained contrast' description without a concrete lighting scenario per appearance
Simple color inversion between light and dark
constraints: Theme file must encode both scenes as distinct semantic color/shadow roles, not a single palette with inverted lightness

decisions.decision: The signature interaction is the cold-launch/New-Game deal: each card leaves the deck with its own individual spring arc (not a uniform cascade), lands with a slight overshoot-and-settle implying weight and a directional highlight catch, then face-up cards perform a genuine two-sided flip around a vertical axis using real card-back/face art, never a cross-dissolve.
decisions.rationale: Restates and makes concrete the earlier product_research/initial_discussion decision that the deal/flip is this app's signature hook and the least forgiving moment in the app since there's no menu screen to hide behind.
rejected_alternatives: A uniform, identical-motion cascade for all cards
A cross-dissolve flip instead of a true two-sided flip
constraints: Deal/flip animation plays only on a genuinely fresh deal (first launch or explicit New Game), never on a resumed cold launch, per DEC-detailed_discussion-003

decisions.decision: Persistence-failure recovery uses one shared, non-blocking pattern across Game, Stats, and Settings with three outcomes (successful restore, fallback-to-default with a visible warning, recoverable error), and on Game specifically the recovery is presented as a normal fresh deal (the signature deal/flip plays exactly as on first install) with a small dismissible banner layered on after the deal settles ('Couldn't restore your last game — dealt a new one') rather than a blocking modal or alert.
decisions.rationale: The app's IA has no menu screen and the deal animation is the least forgiving three seconds in the app; gating a returning player's first view behind a blocking alert dialog would replace 'no menu screen' with something worse, and there is only one honest recovery action anyway (deal fresh), so there's nothing for the user to decide.
rejected_alternatives: A blocking modal/alert on Game launch requiring the user to acknowledge or choose an action before seeing the board
Three fully separate, differently-shaped UI branches for decode failure vs. invalid saved state vs. persistence error
constraints: Settings shows a lightweight toast when settings persistence fails and defaults are substituted
No persistence-failure case may silently present as a normal success/empty state

decisions.decision: The Stats screen must render two structurally distinct visual states for a mode showing zero games: a genuine never-played empty state (inviting icon, on-brand copy like 'No games played in Draw One yet, deal one to start your streak') and a data-loss error state (a different, interruption-style icon, explicit copy stating data was lost rather than never existed, plus a 'Reset local stats and continue' action) — the two must never be visually confusable.
decisions.rationale: Collapsing a real first-use empty state and an actual data-loss event into the same '0 games played' visual would violate the standing no-fabricated-data rule by making data loss indistinguishable from legitimate never-played status.
rejected_alternatives: Using the same empty-state visual language with only longer/different copy to distinguish never-played from data-loss
constraints: Build phase must implement two distinct icon/copy/action treatments for these cases on the Stats screen, not a single template with conditional text

decisions.decision: The default-looking version of this app is explicitly rejected: a plain TabView with system List/Form chrome, SF Symbol suit glyphs reused as both corner pip and suit indicator, flat rounded-rectangle cards with a generic drop shadow on a flat system-color background, and a title/menu screen before entering the game.
decisions.rationale: Phase rules require explicitly naming and rejecting the default-looking option with concrete differences, not adjectives, so the build phase has an unambiguous negative reference.
rejected_alternatives: Describing the rejected default only in general terms ('generic', 'flat') without naming concrete UI elements
constraints: Build phase must implement bespoke embossed glyphs, a custom felt table surface with real lighting/shadow, matte vellum card stock, two art-directed lighting scenes, and a resume/deal-first launch with no interstitial screen

decisions.decision: Card face, stock, and glyph ink colors are fixed constants with zero light/dark variation and zero scene-specific ambient wash or tint of any kind; the daylight-vs-lamplight lighting difference is expressed entirely through the table felt, ambient shadow, and pewter hardware accents, never on the card itself.
decisions.rationale: A card-face wash, even at very low opacity and nominally excluded from the glyph, adds a rendering pass that has to be perfectly scoped away from the glyph on every touch of that view; given the rank/suit legibility gate at ~45-50pt card width is still the single longest-standing untested risk in the entire pipeline, the simplest rule that cannot be gotten wrong beats a richer effect that depends on layering discipline holding forever. The 'different light source' feeling is already achievable via the scene-specific pewter and felt tokens without touching card color at all.
rejected_alternatives: A 2-4% cool-white / 6-8% warm-amber ambient tint wash applied to the card body/border only, excluded from glyph rendering
Full per-scene semantic recoloring of card front/back colors
constraints: Theme.swift must define card.front/back/ink tokens as single fixed constants, not light/dark pairs, and no wash/tint layer may be added in the card rendering pipeline

decisions.decision: Card corner radius is locked at 8pt (radius.card), distinct from pile (10), panel (18), toast (14), button (12), and modal (22) radii.
decisions.rationale: 8pt sits closer to a real playing card's proportional corner cut than a 12pt+ radius (which reads as app-icon-rounded, exactly what design_discussion rejected), while avoiding a physically-accurate ~2.5pt radius that would read as anti-aliasing noise rather than an intentional design choice at true on-screen card size.
rejected_alternatives: 12pt (reads as generic rounded-rect/app-icon)
6pt (initial proposal, revised after both agents did the physical-card-ratio math)
Physically accurate ~2.5-3pt (too small to read as intentional at true device size)
constraints: All card rendering must reference radius.card=8 from Theme.swift, never a literal

decisions.decision: Component naming is locked as: CardView (single renderer for both face-up and face-down states, not CardFaceView), WinOverlay and StuckOverlay as two separate component types (never merged into one TerminalOverlay with an internal enum), and StatsModeFilter (Stats-screen-only, pure local view state, no persistence, no confirmation) kept structurally separate from DrawModeSetting (Settings-screen-only, mutates GameEngine and Settings.json, always routes through DrawModeConfirmSheet) — draw mode has no control surface on the Game screen at all.
decisions.rationale: CardView is more accurate since the same component renders the face-down back state, not just the front. Win and stuck need different iconography, tone, and action sets, and collapsing them into one type with an enum is exactly the kind of accidental simplification that already motivated keeping Stats' never-played/data-loss states structurally separate (DEC-design_discussion-005) — the same risk applies here. Conflating StatsModeFilter and DrawModeSetting into one shared ModeToggle component risked a real correctness bug: a draw-mode change slipping through without the confirmation dialog DEC-app_features-005 requires, since the Stats version has zero side effects and the Settings version mutates real game state.
rejected_alternatives: CardFaceView
A single merged TerminalOverlay component with an internal win/stuck enum
A single shared ModeToggle component used identically across Game header, Stats, and Settings
constraints: Build phase must implement these as distinct named SwiftUI types, not variants of a shared type
Game screen must not include any draw-mode control; it lives only in Settings

decisions.decision: Blocked/rejected-move feedback uses UIImpactFeedbackGenerator(.rigid) plus an 8-12pt one-cycle lateral shake; UINotificationFeedbackGenerator is reserved exclusively for the genuinely rare, significant session events — .success on win and .warning on stuck-board detection.
decisions.rationale: Apple's own HIG guidance is that notification feedback should be used sparingly because frequent use dilutes its perceived meaning; a blocked-move tap is one of the most frequent events in casual play, especially for players still learning legal destinations, so using the heavier notification pattern there would feel naggy within a single session.
rejected_alternatives: UINotificationFeedbackGenerator(.warning) or .error for every blocked move
constraints: All haptic trigger call sites must live in one shared interaction layer, not scattered through view code, per the existing haptics-verification requirement (DEC-prompt_contract-012)

decisions.decision: Reduce Motion fallback is strict: a single 150ms linear opacity-only fade to final position, with zero positional translate and zero per-card stagger, applied identically to the deal sequence, the flip, and move-transit animations.
decisions.rationale: Apple's Reduce Motion guidance targets parallax and positional motion effects specifically because even subtle translation can trigger vestibular discomfort for the people the setting exists for; a per-card stagger is itself a motion/choreography effect a Reduce Motion user is opting out of, not just asking to shorten.
rejected_alternatives: Opacity plus a subtle positional translate
A shortened but still spring-based or staggered deal sequence
constraints: DealOrchestrator must branch on the Reduce Motion environment value once per session and apply this fallback uniformly to deal, flip, and move-transit, not per animation call site

decisions.decision: Stats has no independent per-tab loading state; a single app-level hasFinishedInitialLoad flag, set once after Game/Stats/Settings all restore together at cold start, gates first paint across all three tabs.
decisions.rationale: Once the one cold-start restore completes, Stats reads from an already-in-memory event log with no real async gap when a user taps the tab mid-session; specifying a separate per-tab loading state creates a dead code path that either never fires or, worse, risks getting stuck permanently visible if wired to the wrong lifecycle event — a real bug in the one area (Stats state honesty) this pipeline has repeatedly flagged as must-never-be-wrong.
rejected_alternatives: A dedicated per-tab Stats loading placeholder tied to its own async flag
constraints: Build phase implements one shared hasFinishedInitialLoad flag from the single cold-start restore of GameSave.json, StatsLog.json, and Settings.json, not per-screen loading flags

decisions.decision: Persisted state uses three independently-persisted files (GameSave.json, StatsLog.json, Settings.json), each with its own atomic temp-then-swap write, with a single @Observable GameEngine owning Game state, Stats reading from an append-only local event log the engine writes on game start/end, and Settings owning its own small struct.
decisions.rationale: Physically separate files with independent atomic writes are what actually makes design_discussion's locked requirement (DEC-design_discussion-004: Game, Stats, and Settings each fail and recover independently) hold in practice — a single combined AppState.json would silently reintroduce a shared point of failure where a corrupt game save could take Stats or Settings down with it.
rejected_alternatives: A single combined AppState.json blob for all three screens' persisted state
constraints: Build phase must implement three separate persisted files with independent atomic write-temp-then-swap operations, not a merged state file

decisions.decision: The complete numeric design spec (type scale mapped to Dynamic Type styles, 4pt-base spacing grid, dual light/dark semantic color palettes with fixed card-color constants, corner radii, full component inventory, TabView-only navigation map, per-screen state models, motion/haptics tables, and accessibility rules) is locked as the single canonical handoff for the build phase, superseding both agents' earlier round-1 draft specs and partial component-name lists.
decisions.rationale: The build phase needs exactly one spec with zero invented values and zero duplicate vocabulary; two competing drafts (differing on card color treatment, corner radius, component names, haptic types, and Reduce Motion behavior) would have forced the build phase to silently pick a side or fork into duplicate views.
rejected_alternatives: Handing off both agents' round-1 drafts and letting the build phase reconcile the differences
constraints: Theme.swift must implement every token in this spec directly; no font/size/color/radius literals may appear elsewhere in the view layer

decisions.decision: Core architecture is SwiftUI-only with one main-actor-isolated @Observable GameEngine owning board/undo/timer state, injected via @Environment from the App root, plus separate StatsLogStore and SettingsStore services — Apple frameworks only (SwiftUI, Foundation, Observation, UIKit haptics), no networking framework.
decisions.rationale: Matches the already-locked three-independent-screen persistence model and keeps the app's only stateful mutation surface (GameEngine) isolated from Stats/Settings so a bug in one can't corrupt another; Apple-only frameworks satisfy the permissive-dependency policy with zero review risk.
rejected_alternatives: A shared combined app-state object across Game/Stats/Settings
Introducing any third-party state-management or networking library
constraints: GameEngine must be main-actor-isolated
No URLSession or any networking API anywhere in the codebase

decisions.decision: Persistence uses Codable + FileManager in Application Support (not SwiftData, not UserDefaults for game/stats/settings data), implementing the three-independent-file design (GameSave.json, StatsLog.json, Settings.json) via three separate dedicated actors, one per file, never a shared queue or shared actor.
decisions.rationale: SwiftData's schema/migration machinery is pure overhead for three small Codable structs with no query or relationship needs; UserDefaults would needlessly widen the app's required-reason API surface; a shared write-scheduling actor would silently reintroduce the coupling the three-file split exists to prevent, just moved from the disk layer to the scheduling layer.
rejected_alternatives: SwiftData for game/stats/settings persistence
UserDefaults for game/stats/settings data
One shared PersistenceActor/queue serializing all three files
constraints: Each of the three files must be written through its own independent actor performing temp-write-then-atomic-swap
No SwiftData dependency introduced for this app's persistence

decisions.decision: The undo stack persists as part of GameSave.json itself (full-state log, capped at 200 entries, explicit schema version), not just the current board position.
decisions.rationale: If only current board position survives a crash/jetsam kill, the app silently loses a core safety behavior the player already relies on ('I can always back out mistakes'), which directly contradicts this app's whole positioning of never lying about the player's own state.
rejected_alternatives: Persisting only the current board position and letting undo history reset on relaunch
A delta-based undo log instead of full-state snapshots
constraints: GameSave.json must include a capped, versioned undo history
Full-state snapshots are used for determinism given the small per-entry size at this scale

decisions.decision: Saves are event-driven and debounced: a write fires after every settling state mutation (move, undo, stock draw, timer toggle, session start/end), debounced ~300-500ms per file with a write-coalescing guard skipping no-op writes, plus an unconditional non-debounced flush forced on scenePhase background transition.
decisions.rationale: A scenePhase-only save policy misses a foregrounded jetsam kill or crash after a move has already resolved, which this app has zero excuse to lose; but writing synchronously on every settling sub-event (e.g. a multi-card run relocation) risks I/O-induced stutter during the exact spring animations the app is built to protect, so the write is debounced while the in-memory engine state updates instantly.
rejected_alternatives: Saving only on scenePhase background transitions
Synchronous disk writes on every state-mutating event with no debounce
constraints: In-memory GameEngine state must update immediately for UI regardless of debounce
Background transition must trigger an unconditional flush bypassing the debounce timer

decisions.decision: The rank/suit legibility gate is verified via a required build artifact: a debug-reachable gallery view (or #Preview) rendering all 52 CardViews at the real computed cardWidth formula output, checked up through Dynamic Type accessibility1 before glyph shapes are treated as final.
decisions.rationale: Five consecutive earlier phases flagged card-glyph legibility at true on-device size as an untested, release-blocking risk without ever specifying a concrete verification mechanism; 'check legibility before locking the glyph shapes' is not a testable requirement without a named artifact that must exist in the codebase.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving legibility verification as an unspecified manual check to happen 'at some point' during build
Judging legibility only from zoomed mockups instead of true on-device card width
constraints: Build phase must implement this gallery/preview as an actual artifact in the codebase, gated behind #if DEBUG or an internal QA toggle
Verification must occur at the real cardWidth formula output, not a fixed or zoomed size

decisions.decision: GameEngine's deal function accepts an injectable RandomNumberGenerator defaulting to the system RNG, used solely as a testing seam for deterministic unit-test fixtures; this seam must never be reachable from any production or UI code path.
decisions.rationale: Enables deterministic unit tests (including hand-constructed adversarial draw-3 boards for stuck-detection false-positive testing) without touching the already-locked production rule that every new game uses a fresh real-RNG shuffle with no second deterministic RNG path.
rejected_alternatives: Wiring the injectable RNG to any debug menu or in-app control reachable by a user
constraints: Production deal path must always default to the system RNG
No UI or settings surface may expose or reach the injectable RNG parameter

decisions.decision: Testing strategy includes unit tests over all move-legality rules, win/stuck detection, and exact-state undo restoration; a randomized simulation/fuzz test running thousands of legal moves per draw mode asserting core invariants (52 unique cards always accounted for, foundation ranks never exceed 13, stuck-detection never fires while a legal move exists anywhere); XCUITest coverage of cold-launch deal, blocked-move feedback, both confirmation-sheet paths, and the two structurally distinct Stats states; explicit accessibility identifiers/labels on every custom-rendered view; and Xcode's performAccessibilityAudit() run inside the UI test suite.
decisions.rationale: This is a fully custom-rendered UI with no system List/Form chrome, so none of it inherits accessibility identifiers or VoiceOver behavior automatically; a randomized simulation test is the only mechanism that actually makes the draw-3 'never falsely declare stuck' promise (DEC-app_features-002) verifiable rather than aspirational.
rejected_alternatives: Relying on hand-written unit tests alone without a randomized invariant-checking simulation
Treating accessibility as automatically covered because the app is built in SwiftUI
constraints: Verification phases must run the randomized simulation and treat any invariant violation as a release blocker
All custom views require explicit accessibility identifiers for UI-test hooks, not just VoiceOver labels

decisions.decision: Zero permission usage-description keys, zero entitlements beyond the sandbox default, zero background modes; persistence stays on FileManager rather than UserDefaults to minimize required-reason API surface; a PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy manifest is not authored by default but must be added declaring the specific usage if any code path later touches an actual required-reason API (e.g., reading a file's modification timestamp for stale/corrupt-save detection).
decisions.rationale: Plain FileManager read/write does not itself trigger Apple's required-reason API rules — only specific API categories (file timestamps, disk space, boot time, etc.) do — so mandating a manifest purely because FileManager is used would add unnecessary noise; but the obligation must be tied to actual API usage so it isn't silently skipped if such a call is added later.
rejected_alternatives: Treating a PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy manifest as unconditionally mandatory from day one purely because FileManager is used
Ignoring the manifest requirement entirely regardless of future API usage
constraints: No camera/location/photos/microphone/contacts/network permission keys may be added
If any required-reason API is introduced later, a manifest declaring that exact usage must be authored at that time

decisions.decision: No App Tracking Transparency prompt and no NSUserTrackingUsageDescription key, stated as a deliberate non-requirement rather than an unaddressed gap.
decisions.rationale: The app has genuinely zero tracking of any kind; naming this explicitly forecloses an engineer reflexively adding ATT 'just in case,' which would itself be an unnecessary permission prompt in a zero-permission app.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving ATT unaddressed and letting it be added speculatively later
constraints: No ATT-related API or usage-description key may be added to this app

decisions.decision: No ML/AR framework of any kind (CoreML, CreateML, ARKit, Vision) is in scope for this build, stated as a deliberate exclusion.
decisions.rationale: Naming this explicitly forecloses a 'smart hint solver' or similar feature from sneaking in later as a disguised technical enhancement rather than an intentionally scoped addition requiring its own decision.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving ML/AR framework usage as an unaddressed, implicitly-open question
constraints: Any future ML/AR feature proposal must be raised and scoped as its own decision, not treated as pre-approved

decisions.decision: Zero StoreKit imports, zero payment capability, zero monetization-related entitlements — hard lock consistent with the already-locked no-monetization non-goal.
decisions.rationale: Restates DEC-prompt_contract-010 and DEC-per_app_product_brief-001 at the architecture level so no StoreKit scaffolding or dead paywall code can regress into the codebase.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving StoreKit as an implicitly-absent rather than explicitly-excluded dependency
constraints: No StoreKit framework import or payment capability may be added anywhere in the project

decisions.decision: Zero third-party SwiftPM dependencies, enforced by an actual CI-checkable build step that fails if the project references any package beyond Apple's own frameworks, not merely a stated policy.
decisions.rationale: This fleet has a documented history of shipping dependency-lint failures; a policy statement alone doesn't prevent regression the way an enforced build gate does.
rejected_alternatives: Relying on a written policy alone without an automated enforcement check
constraints: CI must include a step scanning project/package references and failing the build on any non-Apple dependency

decisions.decision: Card.id is a computed String property derived from suit+rank, never a stored Int or UUID field.
decisions.rationale: Single-deck play (locked in prompt_contract) already guarantees suit+rank is a unique, stable identity for all 52 cards; a computed property is structurally excluded from Codable synthesis, so it can never be persisted incorrectly or drift from a save-file bug, which a stored deterministic value (even a derived one) technically still could. It also stays stable across isFaceUp toggling, which matchedGeometryEffect needs for the flip animation to read as one continuous view rather than a destroy/insert cross-dissolve.
rejected_alternatives: A stored UUID generated at deal time
A stored deterministic Int (e.g. suit.rawValue*13+rank.rawValue)
constraints: Card must not gain any stored id field; id is always computed from suit+rank
AnimationStep.cardID and all card-keyed collections use this String id

decisions.decision: PileID.foundation is keyed by Suit, not by an Int index.
decisions.rationale: Makes 'exactly one foundation per suit' a compile-time invariant instead of a runtime bounds check; foundation(7) is simply unrepresentable.
rejected_alternatives: foundation(Int) with a 0..<4 runtime bounds check
constraints: All foundation-indexed logic must pattern-match on Suit, never an array index

decisions.decision: GameState carries no undo/history fields; the undo stack (GameStateSnapshot, full-state, capped at 200) lives only inside GameSaveFile as a plain LIFO stack with no redo cursor.
decisions.rationale: Keeps GameState equality checks (used directly by the fuzz-invariant test suite) free of history bookkeeping, and avoids building a redo cursor field that no phase in this pipeline has ever asked for — a half-wired redo affordance is scope creep dressed as a data structure.
rejected_alternatives: Nesting undoStack/undoCursor inside GameState itself
constraints: Undo pops via popLast() only; no redo mechanism may be added without a new decision reopening this one

decisions.decision: Stats persist as a two-case append-only event stream (StatsEvent.gameStarted written immediately at session start, .gameEnded written on completion/abandonment), with DrawModeStats as a derived, incrementally-updated cache alongside the raw events rather than a per-render recomputation.
decisions.rationale: A single end-of-session struct written only at game-end silently drops an entire session if the app is killed mid-game — exactly the failure mode this app's persistence architecture exists to prevent. Writing gameStarted durably at session start means an abandoned or crashed session still shows up as played instead of vanishing without a trace.
rejected_alternatives: A single StatsEvent struct written once at game completion
Recomputing DrawModeStats from the full event log on every StatsView render
constraints: StatsLogStore.append must update both the event log and the relevant DrawModeStats cache in one write

decisions.decision: RestoreIntegrityService performs a mandatory semantic validation pass (52 unique cards, no duplicate/missing ranks-per-suit, legal face-up stacking, foundation monotonicity) after every successful GameSave.json decode, returning ValidationResult (valid / invalid(reason:)); a failure is classified as PersistenceError.semanticallyInvalid and routed through the existing .dataLoss recovery path (fresh deal + dismissible banner), never silently activated as a resumed game.
decisions.rationale: Atomic writes plus successful Codable decoding only proves the bytes round-tripped, not that the content describes a legal board; a subtle save bug or bit-level corruption could produce valid JSON describing an illegal board, which would then silently poison move-legality and stuck-detection with no visible error. A Bool-only validation result (the initial proposal) can't carry the failure reason the recovery banner needs for honest copy, so the return type must carry a reason string.
rejected_alternatives: Treating successful Codable decode as sufficient proof of a valid save
A Bool-returning validate() with no failure reason
constraints: GameSaveStore.load() must call RestoreIntegrityService.validate before returning .restored
No new UI branch is added — semantic-invalid reuses the existing .dataLoss banner/recovery pattern

decisions.decision: All three persisted files share one PersistenceStore protocol; each conforming actor returns RestoreOutcome<Model> directly from load() (restored / fallbackDefault / dataLoss) rather than throwing, and each actor owns its own independent serial write queue.
decisions.rationale: Encodes design_discussion's required three-way recovery classification at the type level rather than leaving it to caller convention, while preserving the independent-failure guarantee (a slow/corrupt write to one file can never block or corrupt another) all the way from the file-format layer down to the write-scheduling layer.
rejected_alternatives: A protocol with an additional markRecovered() call with no clear caller once RestoreOutcome already carries the failure reason in-band
A single shared actor/queue serializing all three files
constraints: GameSaveStore/StatsLogStore/SettingsStore each conform independently; no shared write queue

decisions.decision: InteractionState is a locked, named finite-state enum (idle / sourceSelected / resolvingMove / dealing / terminal) that all Game-screen view code must read from; no parallel @State booleans for selection, highlight, or ambiguity may be introduced.
decisions.rationale: Without a named FSM type, the natural build-phase shortcut is a handful of @State optionals for selected/highlighted/confirming, which is exactly the pattern that produces 'why didn't the highlight clear' class bugs — especially costly here since there's no menu screen to hide a rough edge behind.
rejected_alternatives: Ad-hoc @State booleans/optionals scattered across GameView for selection and highlight tracking
constraints: GameView and all its subviews must derive selection/highlight/ambiguity rendering from GameEngine.interaction, not independent view state

decisions.decision: DealOrchestrator/AnimationPlan is a locked, pure (side-effect-free) animation-planning layer that produces a declarative plan consumed by GameView via matchedGeometryEffect keyed on Card.id, covering fresh deal, flip, and multi-card run-relocation transit.
decisions.rationale: A pure planning layer is unit-testable independently of whether SwiftUI actually renders it smoothly — 'did we compute the right animation sequence' and 'did it render smoothly' are different failure modes, and only the first is testable without a running app. matchedGeometryEffect keyed on stable card identity is also what makes a multi-card run relocation read as one coherent physical unit instead of N cards racing each other to nearby points.
rejected_alternatives: Independently-animated per-view offsets with no shared planning layer
Wiring animation logic directly and untested inside GameView
constraints: DealOrchestrator must branch on Reduce Motion once per session and apply the locked strict opacity-only fallback uniformly across deal/flip/transit

decisions.decision: Stuck detection is implemented as two separate, independently-testable types (DrawOneStuckDetector, DrawThreeStuckDetector) behind one StuckDetector protocol, selected by GameEngine based on the active draw mode.
decisions.rationale: Operationalizes DEC-detailed_discussion-004 and DEC-app_features-002, which already require draw-1's exact static pass and draw-3's conservative approximation to be distinct algorithms with different false-positive risk profiles; a single detectStuck() method would blur that distinction and make the two impossible to fuzz-test independently.
rejected_alternatives: A single GameEngine.detectStuck() method branching internally on draw mode
constraints: The fuzz/simulation test suite must exercise both detector types independently, with a specific adversarial test proving DrawThreeStuckDetector never false-positives

decisions.decision: Ambiguous-destination VoiceOver exposure is a named type, DestinationAccessibilityAction, built from InteractionState.sourceSelected's legalDestinations and wired as discrete .accessibilityAction entries.
decisions.rationale: Operationalizes the already-locked requirement (DEC-detailed_discussion-002, design_handoff accessibility rules) that a tap resolving to multiple legal destinations must expose each as a discrete VoiceOver action, not just a visual highlight — this had been stated as a requirement but never given a concrete type until this phase.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving ambiguous-destination VoiceOver exposure as an implementation detail with no named contract type
constraints: CardView/PileSlotView must build their .accessibilityAction handlers from this type, driven directly off InteractionState

decisions.decision: Module layout is locked as App/, DesignSystem/, Domain/, Persistence/, Features/Game/, Features/Stats/, Features/Settings/, Interaction/, DebugTools/, with Domain having zero dependency on SwiftUI or Persistence and Persistence knowing only Codable structs.
decisions.rationale: This is the boundary that lets parallel build lanes work independently — Domain logic is fully unit-testable without a view hierarchy, and a persistence bug can't leak UI concerns or vice versa.
rejected_alternatives: A flatter structure without an enforced Domain/Persistence/UI dependency direction
constraints: Domain/ must not import SwiftUI; Persistence/ must not import Domain's UI-facing types

decisions.decision: The card-glyph legibility gate (Theme tokens, CardGlyphs, CardView, CardGalleryDebugView) is sequenced as its own milestone that must close before gameplay UI (GameView/DealOrchestrator) construction begins, rather than being bundled into a later visual-polish milestone after gameplay UX.
